title: Essentials of Networking
subtitle: Climb the money ladder -- one networking question per grade level

gradeLabels.f: F-RANK -- Back to the Patch Panel

questions.q: What does a VLAN (Virtual LAN) do on a managed switch?
options: Assigns a dedicated IP address to each port
Logically segments the switch into separate broadcast domains
Increases available bandwidth by bonding ports together
questions.note: VLANs create logical boundaries on a switch; 802.1Q tags carry VLAN identity across trunk links.

explain.correct: A VLAN logically divides a single physical switch into multiple isolated broadcast domains. Frames tagged with 802.1Q carry VLAN membership across trunk links, so broadcasts stay within their VLAN.
wrong: VLANs do not encrypt traffic. That is the job of protocols such as MACsec or IPsec.
VLANs do not assign IP addresses to ports. IP addressing is handled by the Layer 3 network or a DHCP server.
Port-channel (link aggregation / 802.3ad) bonds ports for bandwidth. VLANs are a Layer 2 segmentation mechanism, not a bandwidth feature.

questions.q: Which network device makes forwarding decisions based on a CAM table of learned MAC-address-to-port mappings?
questions.note: A switch learns MAC addresses from incoming frames and records them in its Content Addressable Memory (CAM) table.

explain.correct: A switch examines the source MAC of every incoming frame and records it with the ingress port in its CAM table. Future unicast frames destined for a known MAC are forwarded only out the correct port.
wrong: A router operates at Layer 3 and makes decisions based on IP destination addresses and a routing table, not a MAC CAM table.
A hub is a Layer 1 device with no intelligence; it floods every incoming signal out all ports unconditionally.
A wireless access point manages wireless associations but still relies on an upstream switch's CAM table for wired forwarding decisions.

questions.q: Which Wi-Fi security standard is currently recommended for new deployments and uses the SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) handshake?
questions.note: The Wi-Fi security evolution is WEP (broken RC4) -> WPA (TKIP) -> WPA2 (AES-CCMP) -> WPA3 (SAE, current recommended).

explain.correct: WPA3 replaced the PSK handshake with SAE, which provides forward secrecy and is resistant to offline dictionary attacks. It is the current Wi-Fi Alliance recommended standard.
wrong: WEP uses RC4 with static keys and 24-bit IVs. It is cryptographically broken and was deprecated in 2004.
WPA used TKIP as a stopgap fix for WEP weaknesses. TKIP is also considered insecure and was deprecated in 2012.
WPA2 introduced AES-CCMP and is still widely deployed, but it is vulnerable to PMKID and offline dictionary attacks against the 4-way handshake. WPA3 is the current recommendation.

questions.q: A standard IP access control list (ACL, numbered 1-99) filters traffic based on which criterion?
options: Source IP, destination IP, and destination port (all three)
questions.note: Standard ACLs (1-99) match source IP only and are placed near the destination; extended ACLs (100-199) match source+destination+port and are placed near the source.

explain.correct: Standard ACLs inspect only the source IP address field of the packet. Because they cannot restrict by destination, they are placed as close to the destination as possible to avoid blocking traffic unnecessarily.
wrong: Filtering by destination port is a Layer 4 criterion available only in extended ACLs (numbered 100-199 or named).
ACLs operate at Layer 3 and above. MAC addresses are a Layer 2 concern handled by tools such as port security or MAC ACLs on specific platforms, not standard IP ACLs.
Matching source IP, destination IP, and port simultaneously describes an extended ACL, not a standard ACL.

questions.q: A network engineer assigns a /26 subnet. How many USABLE host addresses does this subnet provide?

explain.correct: A /26 mask leaves 6 host bits. 2^6 = 64 total addresses, minus the network address and directed broadcast = 62 usable host addresses.
wrong: 64 is the total number of addresses in a /26 block, not the usable count. You must subtract 2 (network + broadcast) to get usable hosts.
30 usable hosts corresponds to a /27 subnet (2^5 - 2 = 30), which is half the size of a /26.
126 usable hosts corresponds to a /25 subnet (2^7 - 2 = 126), which is twice the size of a /26.

questions.q: What is the correct order of messages in the DHCP DORA process?
questions.note: DHCP DORA: client broadcasts Discover, server unicasts/broadcasts Offer, client broadcasts Request, server sends Acknowledge. UDP ports 67 (server) and 68 (client).

explain.correct: DORA is the mnemonic: Discover (client broadcast seeking a server), Offer (server proposes an IP), Request (client formally requests that IP), Acknowledge (server confirms the lease). The exchange uses UDP 67/68.
wrong: Placing Request before Offer is impossible; the client cannot request a specific IP until the server has offered one.
This order is entirely incorrect. The client must initiate with a Discover before any Offer can be made.
The client cannot send a Request as the very first message because it does not yet know which server or IP address to request.

questions.q: An IPv6 link-local address is automatically assigned to every IPv6-enabled interface. Which prefix does it always begin with?
questions.note: Link-local addresses (fe80::/10) are non-routable and scoped to the local link. Every IPv6 interface auto-configures one using EUI-64 or a random suffix.

explain.correct: Link-local addresses fall in the fe80::/10 range (fe80 through febf). They are automatically generated on every IPv6 interface, used for neighbor discovery and routing protocols on the local link, and are never forwarded by routers.
wrong: 2000::/3 is the Global Unicast Address (GUA) range -- routable addresses assigned by ISPs and regional registries, analogous to public IPv4 addresses.
ff00::/8 is the IPv6 multicast range, used for one-to-many communication (e.g., ff02::1 for all nodes on a link).
::1/128 is the IPv6 loopback address, equivalent to 127.0.0.1 in IPv4. It is a host-only address, not a link-local prefix.

questions.q: Which type of firewall maintains a state table of active connections and automatically permits return traffic without an explicit inbound rule?
questions.note: Stateful inspection tracks TCP/UDP session state; return traffic matching an existing entry is auto-allowed. Packet filters are stateless and must have explicit rules for both directions.

explain.correct: A stateful inspection firewall records source/destination IP, port, and TCP state in a connection table. When an internal host initiates a session, the return traffic from the remote host is automatically matched to that entry and allowed, requiring no separate inbound rule.
wrong: A packet-filtering (stateless) firewall evaluates each packet in isolation against a static rule set. It has no memory of prior packets, so return traffic requires an explicit permit rule in both directions.
An application-layer proxy can inspect content deeply but does not specifically define the 'stateful inspection' mechanism that auto-allows return traffic at the session layer.

NAT translates addresses but is not a firewall type. While a NAT gateway incidentally blocks unsolicited inbound traffic by lacking a mapping, it does not implement stateful inspection as a security policy mechanism.

questions.q: For optimal ACL placement, where should an EXTENDED ACL be placed, and where should a STANDARD ACL be placed?
options: Extended near the SOURCE interface; standard near the DESTINATION interface
Both types should always be placed at the core router only
Standard near the SOURCE interface; extended near the DESTINATION interface
Extended near the DESTINATION interface; standard near the SOURCE interface
questions.note: Extended ACLs (src+dst+port) go near the source to discard unwanted traffic early. Standard ACLs (source IP only) go near the destination to avoid accidentally blocking that source from reaching other destinations.

explain.correct: Extended ACLs specify source, destination, and port -- placing them near the source stops unwanted traffic immediately, conserving bandwidth across the network. Standard ACLs match only source IP, so placing them near the source could inadvertently block that source from reaching ALL other destinations; placing them near the destination limits the scope of denial.
wrong: Placing all ACLs only at the core violates the principle of filtering as close to the origin as possible for extended ACLs, and wastes bandwidth carrying traffic that could have been dropped earlier.
This is the reversed, incorrect rule. Standard ACLs near the source would block the source from ALL destinations network-wide, which is almost never the intent.
Placing extended ACLs near the destination allows unwanted traffic to traverse the entire network before being dropped, wasting bandwidth and router CPU.

questions.q: An administrator applies a wildcard mask of 0.0.0.255 in an ACL statement. Which addresses does this mask match?
options: Any address where the last three octets can be any value (first octet fixed)
Only the exact single IP address specified (no wildcarding)
Any address where the FIRST THREE octets match exactly (last octet is any value)
Any address where the first octet matches exactly (last three octets are any value)
questions.note: In a wildcard mask, 0 = must match, 255 = any value. 0.0.0.255 means the first three octets must match exactly; the fourth can be 0-255.

explain.correct: Wildcard mask bits work as follows: 0 means the corresponding bit in the address MUST match; 255 (all 1s) means the bit can be anything. With 0.0.0.255, the first three octets are fixed (must match the ACL source address) and the fourth octet is completely free, matching all 256 values in that octet -- equivalent to a /24 subnet.
wrong: A wildcard of 255.255.255.0 would fix only the first octet and free the last three, which is the opposite of 0.0.0.255.
A wildcard of 0.0.0.0 (or the keyword 'host') matches exactly one IP address. 0.0.0.255 is not a host wildcard.
A wildcard of 0.255.255.255 would fix only the first octet. 0.0.0.255 fixes the FIRST THREE octets, not just the first.

questions.q: A switch port's port-security is triggered by an unknown MAC address. Which violation mode err-disables the port, generates a syslog message AND an SNMP trap, and is considered the most secure option?
questions.note: Protect silently drops frames (no logging). Restrict drops frames + increments the violation counter + sends a syslog/SNMP notification. Shutdown err-disables the port entirely -- the most secure and most disruptive mode.

explain.correct: Shutdown (the default violation mode) immediately places the port into an err-disabled state, sends a syslog message, and generates an SNMP trap. The port must be manually re-enabled (or auto-recovery configured). Because it removes the attacker's network access entirely rather than just dropping frames, it is the most secure mode.
wrong: Protect silently discards frames from unauthorized MAC addresses but does NOT increment the violation counter, send a syslog message, or generate an SNMP trap. The administrator has no visibility that a violation occurred.

Restrict drops frames from unauthorized MACs AND increments the violation counter and sends a syslog/SNMP notification -- but it keeps the port UP and operational. It is more visible than Protect but less secure than Shutdown because the port remains active.
'Block' is not a valid Cisco IOS port-security violation mode. The three valid modes are protect, restrict, and shutdown.
